reference.source: RCOG guidance on ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome / reproductive medicine texts
clinicalPearls: OHSS is an iatrogenic complication of ovarian stimulation, usually triggered by hCG exposure for oocyte maturation or by an early pregnancy
The central mechanism is increased vascular permeability with fluid shifting from the intravascular space into third spaces such as the peritoneal and pleural cavities
Risk is higher in young women, those with polycystic ovaries, high antral follicle counts, and a strong response with high oestradiol
Early OHSS presents within days of the trigger, while late OHSS occurring after implantation tends to be more severe and prolonged
Clinical features range from bloating and abdominal discomfort to tense ascites, breathlessness, oliguria, and haemoconcentration
Major hazards are venous thromboembolism from haemoconcentration and hypercoagulability, and hypovolaemia with renal impairment
Management is largely supportive with fluid balance, symptom relief, thromboprophylaxis, and paracentesis for tense ascites in severe cases
Prevention through tailored stimulation, agonist triggers, and elective embryo freezing has reduced severe disease
reference.pathophysiology: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome arises when multiple stimulated follicles, under the influence of hCG, release vasoactive mediators, notably vascular endothelial growth factor, that increase capillary permeability. Protein-rich fluid leaks from the circulation into the peritoneal, pleural, and occasionally pericardial spaces, producing ascites, effusions, and intravascular volume depletion. The resulting haemoconcentration and stasis, compounded by the hypercoagulable state of stimulation and early pregnancy, predispose to thromboembolism, while reduced renal perfusion causes oliguria and electrolyte disturbance. Ongoing hCG stimulation, including from an implanting pregnancy, sustains and worsens the process.
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count with haematocrit to assess haemoconcentration
Coagulation screen and assessment of thrombosis risk
Pelvic ultrasound to measure ovarian size and detect ascites
Chest imaging or echocardiography if effusions or breathlessness are present
redFlags: Severe breathlessness or hypoxia from large effusions or thromboembolism
Signs of venous or arterial thrombosis, including limb swelling or neurological deficit
Oliguria, rising creatinine, or marked haemoconcentration
Tense ascites with haemodynamic compromise or acute abdomen suggesting torsion
reference.prognosis: Most cases are mild to moderate and resolve spontaneously, particularly when not compounded by pregnancy. Severe and critical OHSS can be life-threatening through thromboembolism, renal failure, and respiratory compromise, but outcomes are generally good with timely supportive care and thromboprophylaxis.
pitfalls: Omitting thromboprophylaxis despite marked haemoconcentration and hypercoagulability
Aggressive crystalloid loading without addressing the underlying capillary leak
Missing ovarian torsion in enlarged stimulated ovaries with worsening pain
Underestimating late, pregnancy-associated OHSS, which can be more severe and protracted
